proposals.name: Names an incumbent's failure and derives the fix from it
proposals.instruction: Score how tightly the proposed change is bound to a diagnosed defect in something people already use. 10 = the abstract identifies a specific existing method or standard practice, states precisely where and why it breaks (a named regime, a named pathology, a named structural requirement), and the proposed change is the direct consequence of that diagnosis, so a reader can see the fix could not have been arrived at without the diagnosis. 5 = a limitation of prior work is asserted generically ('existing methods struggle with X') and a plausible remedy is offered, but the link is loose. 0 = a method is proposed with no account of what specifically was wrong before, or the stated deficiency is only 'this has not been tried yet'. Do not reward mere criticism of prior work; reward diagnosis-to-remedy entailment.
proposals.rationale: The strongest dense_high_card_low rows are all diagnosis-driven: R01 shows LARS fails specifically on attention models and then builds the layerwise adaptation that repairs exactly that; R19 names two concrete GCN defects (needs test data present at training; recursive neighborhood expansion) and its integral-transform reformulation removes both; R46 enumerates three internal DNC pathologies (no key-value separation, de-allocation aliasing, linkage-chain degradation) and fixes each; R55 shows LOLA's 'arrogant' non-convergence and constructs SOS to inherit the missing guarantee. A scorecard built from generic criteria will credit 'proposes a new method' equally for a method with and without this entailment, so it flattens exactly the property the dense model appears to be reading.

proposals.name: Improved formal bound stated against the explicit prior bound
proposals.instruction: Score the presence and sharpness of a formal result that is positioned against the best previously known result. 10 = the abstract gives a concrete rate, complexity, or sample/query/deployment bound, gives the competing prior bound it improves on (by name, citation, or explicit expression), and says in what respect the improvement is optimal or near-optimal. 5 = a bound or guarantee is stated but with no prior bound to compare it to. 0 = no formal quantity at all, or 'we provide theoretical analysis' with no statement of what is bounded. Judge only what is written; a bound in symbols with its predecessor beside it is the high end even if no experiment is described.
proposals.rationale: R49 states an O(m + poly(k/eps)) coreset against an exponential dependence (Feldman and Schulman) and a weaker bi-criteria guarantee (Huang et al.), and argues near-optimality of the m dependence; R24 states O~(d^2 H^5 / eps^2) trajectories within H deployments and claims first simultaneous optimality in deployment complexity and d; R25 replaces O(C^2 L^5) with O(C L^4) and O(C L^3 log L). These carry the three lowest card percentiles in the slice (.021, .009, .120) against mid-to-high dense values, which is what you would expect if the criterion bank has no place to put a bound-versus-bound comparison and defaults such papers to 'no benchmarks, no ablations, no code'.

proposals.name: Contribution by subtraction: removes standard machinery, keeps performance
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work's advance consists in showing that an accepted component is unnecessary. 10 = the abstract identifies a component the field routinely includes, removes or freezes it, and reports that quality is preserved or improved without it, with the removal itself as the headline claim. 5 = the method is simpler than prior work as a side benefit but the claim rests on added machinery. 0 = the contribution is purely additive: new modules, losses, or stages stacked onto an existing pipeline, with no element eliminated. A simplification that costs accuracy but is honest about the trade may still score 6-8; a simplification claimed without any indication of what performance survived scores at most 4.
proposals.rationale: R02's entire claim is that the VGG perceptual loss becomes superfluous once the discriminator is re-cast as a segmentation network; R06 argues the final affine classifier can be fixed up to a global scale with little or no accuracy loss; R44 derives a Simple Spectral Graph Convolution competitive with a linear learner. All three sit high on dense and low on card (.868/.372, .722/.248, .618/.141). A criterion bank naturally rewards visible apparatus, so removal of apparatus reads to it as a thin contribution while an expert reads it as the more expensive result to obtain.

proposals.name: Reusable primitive versus single-application pipeline
proposals.instruction: Score how far the introduced object travels beyond the paper's own experiments. 10 = the contribution is a drop-in general-purpose building block (an estimator, an optimizer, a layer, a regularizer, a verifier) whose interface is stated such that unrelated systems could adopt it without adopting the rest of the paper. 6 = a method general within one problem family. 0 = a pipeline assembled and tuned for a single task, dataset family, or application domain, where transfer is not addressed. Judge the object, not the number of datasets it was tested on: a primitive tested once still scores high; a pipeline tested on ten benchmarks in one domain still scores low.
proposals.rationale: R20 (a categorical gradient estimator), R01 (an optimizer with a public implementation), and R41 (a defense applicable to pretrained networks with no fine-tuning) are all dense-high and card-lower, and all three are objects other papers can pick up whole. Against them, R54 builds a lane-occupancy interaction module for vehicle trajectory prediction and R15 analyzes a CNN for zebrafish swim-bout classification, both dense-low with card notably higher (.517/.842 and .158/.756). A criterion bank scores what was done in the paper; reusability is a property of what leaves the paper.

proposals.name: Load-bearing premise established rather than assumed
proposals.instruction: Locate the single assumption the method most depends on, then score whether the abstract does anything to establish it. 10 = the premise is proved, or demonstrated by a reported phenomenon or synthetic construction, before the method is built on it. 5 = the premise is plausible and explicitly flagged as an assumption, and its violation is discussed. 0 = the premise is introduced with 'assuming that', 'under the assumption that', or 'we hypothesize that' and is then used as the justification for the entire design, with no evidence offered and no consequences of its failure named. Penalize most heavily when the assumption is precisely the thing the results would test.
proposals.rationale: R54 designs its interaction model 'assuming that agents passing adjacent lanes will highly interact', R18 sets its learning pace 'under the assumption that less uncertain samples should be more strongly driving the training', and R05 rests on 'we hypothesize that the optimal strategy for training surrogates is to preserve the ranks' - all three are dense-low with high card (.842, .833, .825). Contrast R31, which proves stability and non-dissipativity before claiming long-range propagation, and R23, which explicitly reports experiments supporting its complexity hypothesis before deriving a score from it. A bank criterion for 'clearly stated motivation' will read the assumption sentence as a virtue; an expert reads a bare assumption in the load-bearing position as the weakest joint in the paper.

proposals.name: Gain contingent on a knob the abstract itself concedes
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the reported benefit is presented as available without per-problem tuning. 10 = the improvement is claimed to hold with the same setting across the reported conditions, or the method is explicitly parameter-free, or reduced tuning is itself part of the claim. 5 = tuning is normal and unremarked. 0 = the abstract's own wording makes the gain conditional on choosing the right value ('with an appropriate X', 'for a suitable choice of', 'we explore methods to stabilize') without saying how that value is obtained without access to the answer. Score from the abstract's own hedges, not from what you imagine the full paper contains.
proposals.rationale: R03 concedes that 'using an appropriate beta largely mitigates the issue', which relocates the contribution from a fix to a knob; R29 must add perturbations of the amalgamation target to keep its own process from being high-variance; R26 introduces a regularization function designed to encourage encodings with certain properties, i.e. a second search problem inside the first. All three are dense-low with much higher card (.641, .637, .932). In the opposite direction, R01 advertises 'very little hyperparameter tuning' and R23 advertises a 'parameter-free' score, both with lower card than dense. A criterion bank rewards the presence of a mechanism; it has no slot for a mechanism whose value must be found per problem.

proposals.name: Magnitude with a named comparator, not intensifiers or bare counts
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the abstract's empirical claim can be checked from its own wording. 10 = at least one headline result carries a number, its unit, and the thing it is measured against (before/after, ours/named baseline, old bound/new bound), such that a reader could falsify it. 5 = numbers are given but the comparator is unnamed ('improves by 3 points' over unspecified baselines), or a comparator is named without a magnitude. 0 = the empirical claim is carried entirely by intensifiers ('significant superiority', 'remarkable gain', 'consistently outperform', 'substantial improvements') or by counts of experimental apparatus (number of baselines, datasets, tasks) with no effect size anywhere.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high side states magnitudes flatly: R01 (3 days to 76 minutes, batch 32868), R04 (two to four times fewer queries, fail two to five times less often), R46 (43% mean error reduction on bAbI), R59 (adversarial examples for 4.38% of samples at eps=0.1, certificates for the rest). The dense-low, card-high side leans on intensifiers and counts: R38 ('significant superiority over baselines'), R54 ('remarkable performance gain'), R05 ('12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks' with 'new state-of-the-art' and no effect size), R22 ('consistently outperform' over 6 long-text and 8 short-text datasets). Breadth counts are the easiest thing for a fixed criterion bank to reward and the least informative about size of effect.

proposals.name: Mechanism explained by derivation, not by analogy
proposals.instruction: Score the type of explanation offered for why the method should work. 10 = the mechanism is derived: an identity, reformulation, expansion, or spectral/geometric analysis is stated in the abstract and the method falls out of it, so the design choices are consequences rather than options. 5 = the mechanism is described operationally (what the modules do) without argument for why it should help. 0 = the only offered justification is an analogy to biology, human cognition, systems engineering, or another field, with the analogy doing the explanatory work and no formal or empirical bridge from analogy to design. Metaphor used only as naming color, with a real derivation present, does not lower the score.
proposals.rationale: R19 interprets graph convolutions as integral transforms under probability measures, which then licenses Monte Carlo estimation and importance sampling; R44 gives a spectral analysis showing its operator is a low-pass/high-pass trade-off; R32 models quantization as an l-infinity bounded perturbation so the first-order loss term is regularized by the l1 norm of gradients - all dense-high, card-low. Against them, R36 justifies its allocation scheme by heap allocation and the complementary learning systems theory of human memory, and R09 justifies policy crossover by natural selection; both are dense-low with higher card (.581, .778). Analogy reads as 'well-motivated' to a criterion bank and as unearned to an expert.

proposals.name: Earned surprise: a stated tension the paper resolves
proposals.instruction: Score whether the result is one the informed reader would not have predicted from the setup, with the abstract making the tension explicit. 10 = the abstract sets up a reason to expect the opposite (an optimality result, a component believed necessary, a phenomenon believed to require a different regime) and then reports the contrary finding with the mechanism that dissolves the tension. 5 = the result is nonobvious but not framed against any expectation. 0 = the result is the expected consequence of the intervention (an added module improves the metric it was added to improve), with nothing at stake in the outcome.
proposals.rationale: R04 first proves current black-box attacks are optimal in a natural sense and then beats them by importing information from outside the model (gradient priors) - the setup makes its own result look impossible; R06 turns a parameter block everyone trains into one nobody needs to; R02 shows the standard auxiliary loss is dispensable rather than merely improvable; R50 recovers double descent under minimal assumptions on the parametric form where the phenomenon was thought to need linear/kernel proxies. All four are dense-high with card far lower (.222, .248, .372, .047). By contrast R34 (layer attention raises accuracy) and R18 (uncertainty-weighted pacing helps) deliver the expected direction and sit at card .970 and .833. A fixed bank scores whether a result is reported, not whether it was at risk.

proposals.name: Unlocks a new regime or capability versus a better number in the same regime
proposals.instruction: Score what becomes possible that was not possible before. 10 = the abstract states a capability or operating regime that was previously out of reach - a scale, a class of objects that can now be specified or verified, a first exact determination, a training budget that changes how the work is done - and makes the previous limit explicit. 6 = a substantial efficiency gain within the existing regime. 0 = the same task, same metric, same regime, with a higher number. Speed-ups count as regime change only when the abstract says what the speed-up now permits.
proposals.rationale: R01 does not merely speed BERT training, it moves it from 3 days to 76 minutes at the memory limit of a TPU pod; R59 verifies networks with an order of magnitude more ReLUs than any complete verifier and determines an exact adversarial accuracy for the first time; R13 makes it possible to specify priors as Gaussian or implicit stochastic processes rather than over weights; R33 makes perturbation sets learnable rather than hand-specified. All are dense-high with card well below (.662, .402, .034, .068). Against them R17 and R34 report better numbers on Atari 100k and ImageNet-scale vision within the existing regime at card .936 and .970. Regime change requires knowing where the old ceiling was, which a per-criterion judge reading one abstract in isolation is poorly placed to score.

proposals.name: Content-to-apparatus ratio in the abstract itself
proposals.instruction: Score what fraction of the abstract's persuasive weight is carried by substantive claims rather than scaffolding. 10 = nearly every sentence advances a claim - the object, its mechanism, its consequence - with background compressed to the minimum needed and no roadmap. 5 = a normal mix, with a paragraph of setup and a paragraph of results. 0 = much of the text is restated background, enumerated roadmaps ('our contributions are three-fold; first... next... finally...'), component inventories, submission boilerplate (ethics acknowledgements, one-sentence summaries), and release links, with the actual mechanism compressed into one vague sentence. Score the ratio, not the length: a long abstract dense with claims scores high, a short abstract of pure setup scores low.
proposals.rationale: R27 is three sentences, no background, no roadmap, and carries the highest dense value in the slice at .996 against card .355; R04, R20, and R48 are similarly compressed and all sit dense-high with card at .222, .551, .192. At the other end, R38 spends its length on a three-fold contribution list and a component inventory (i, ii, iii) at card .594, R22 restates its two challenges at length at card .679, and R57 ends with literal submission boilerplate ('Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge...', 'One-sentence Summary:') at card .906 against dense .605. Countable scaffolding is exactly what a fixed criterion bank can see, and it is close to orthogonal to how much is being claimed.

proposals.name: Theory and experiment bear on the same claim
proposals.instruction: Score whether the formal and empirical halves are about one thing. 10 = a guarantee is proved about the proposed object and the experiments test the property that guarantee is about (prove non-dissipativity, then show deep stacks train; prove convergence, then show it converges where the prior method did not). 5 = both halves are present but concern different properties, e.g. theory about a simplified proxy and experiments about leaderboard accuracy. 0 = only one half is present with the other gestured at, e.g. a claimed advantage with no evidence of either kind, or 'extensive experiments' with a mechanism that was never argued. A theory-only paper whose theory is the whole claim should be scored under A02, not penalized here below 5.
proposals.rationale: R01 gives convergence analysis for LAMB and LARS in nonconvex settings and then shows the large-batch training the analysis is about; R31 proves stability and non-dissipativity and then shows dozens of layers train effectively, which is the empirical shadow of exactly that proof; R13 proves the KL between stochastic processes equals the supremum of marginal KLs and then uses finite measurement sets in the training objective that identity licenses; R55 proves local convergence and saddle avoidance and then matches or beats LOLA. All four are dense-high and card-lower. Against them R39 argues lower-variance, integrator-free, embarrassingly parallel estimation with no empirical anchor named at all (dense .060), and R09 offers no argument for why imitation-based crossover should work beyond the genetic analogy (card .778). Coupling is invisible to criteria that score 'has theory' and 'has experiments' separately.

proposals.name: Produces an instrument that makes other people's claims checkable
proposals.instruction: Score whether the contribution is measurement infrastructure rather than a competitor entry. 10 = the output is a tool that adjudicates claims made by others - a verifier, a certificate, an attack that establishes upper bounds on robustness, a dataset or protocol that separates a confound - and the abstract says what it now lets the community determine. 6 = the work supplies a diagnostic that applies beyond its own method. 0 = the output only raises the authors' own score on an existing benchmark and produces nothing another group could use to test a third party's claim.
proposals.rationale: The slice's adversarial-evaluation cluster is uniformly dense-high and card-low: R59 (mixed integer verifier producing exact adversarial accuracy and certificates, .987/.402), R48 (meta-gradient attacks that bound what GNNs can withstand, .925/.192), R45 (a first-order gradient attack generator proposed as NLP's missing PGD-equivalent, .748/.333), R04 (query-efficient black-box attacks, .688/.222). R11 belongs here too - counterfactually-revised data is an instrument for detecting spurious-feature reliance in other people's classifiers, .618/.295. Against them, R34 and R60 improve or re-represent networks without producing anything that tests a third party. A criterion bank scores accuracy and novelty of the method; it has no place to record that a paper changed what the field can measure.

proposals.name: Transferable finding about the phenomenon, not only about the artifact
proposals.instruction: Score whether a reader who never adopts the method still learns something durable. 10 = the abstract reports a fact about the domain, models in general, or the problem structure that survives the paper's specific artifact, and states it precisely enough to be checked or contradicted later. 5 = an observation about the phenomenon appears but is entangled with the proposed system. 0 = every claim is of the form 'our system scores higher than theirs', with nothing asserted about the world outside the comparison.
proposals.rationale: R11 reports that classifiers trained on original data fail on counterfactually-revised counterparts and vice versa, and that combined training removes sensitivity to genre mentions - facts about learned text classifiers that outlive the dataset being released (.618/.295); R50 reports that the loss function shapes double descent in finite-width networks and ties it to the Hessian spectrum at the optimum (.389/.047); R57 reports that 10-30% language-specific computation at the top and/or bottom layers is where the capacity matters and that one-to-many benefits more than many-to-one. Against them R34 and R54 assert only relative standing. A bank criterion for 'contribution' counts the artifact; the transferable fact is a different currency.

proposals.name: Prior work engaged specifically enough to be checked
proposals.instruction: Score the resolution at which the abstract locates itself against existing work. 10 = the relevant prior methods or results are named individually (method name, author, venue, or explicit bound) and the abstract says precisely what each one gets and where this work departs, so a reader could verify the positioning without the body. 5 = a named family of approaches is engaged, but the specific competitors are 'existing methods' or 'the state of the art'. 0 = prior work appears only as an undifferentiated mass to be outperformed, or the only positioning is that a gap exists because nobody has tried this. Naming one's own baselines is not the same as naming what they achieve.
proposals.rationale: R49 places its coreset against Feldman and Schulman (SODA'12), Huang et al. (FOCS'18), and Braverman et al. (FOCS'22) with what each gives and what it costs; R19 names Kipf and Welling and the exact assumption of their setup; R55 names LOLA and LookAhead and what each does and fails to do; R01 names LARS and the task where it degrades. These sit at card .021, .209, .060, .662 with dense at .474, .904, .342, .979. Against them R38 positions itself against 'the existing works', R34 against 'many state-of-the-art vision networks', and R54 against 'existing methods... using pooling, attention, or graph-based methods' - all card-high. Specific engagement is costly and evidences that the authors know the literature at the level of results rather than of topics; a fixed bank sees only that related work is mentioned.

proposals.name: Sheer verbal bulk of the abstract
proposals.instruction: Estimate only how much text there is and how densely sub-claims are packed into it: approximate word count, number of sentences, and number of distinct sub-claims stacked up. Score 0 for a very short, spare abstract (roughly under 100 words, one or two claims, as in a single compact paragraph); score 5 for a typical mid-length abstract; score 10 for a very long, densely packed abstract (roughly 300 words or more, many stacked clauses, several separately announced sub-results). This is a measurement of verbal bulk ONLY. The judge must NOT decide whether the length is appropriate, whether the prose is well written, whether the coverage is thorough, or whether the underlying work is good. A short abstract and a long abstract can both be excellent research; only the extent of text is being scored here.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1. Length separates the two halves of this slice almost by inspection. The extreme dense-high side is terse: R46 is roughly three sentences (dense_pct=0.996, card_pct=0.355), R22 is one short paragraph (0.699 vs 0.145), R23 is compact (0.880 vs 0.551), R20 (0.688 vs 0.222). The card-high side is bulky: R12 runs to a three-fold contribution recital (0.291 vs 0.594), R26 (0.333 vs 0.679), R08 (0.372 vs 0.675). A bank of 0-10 criteria scored independently and then summed mechanically rewards any abstract that gives each criterion something to latch onto, which longer text does automatically; word count is not research quality.

proposals.name: Inline mathematical notation and complexity-bound density
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the abstract's visible surface is occupied by inline mathematical notation rather than prose: LaTeX-style symbols and macros, named spaces and sets, big-O or order expressions, epsilon / delta / d / k / H parameters, subscripted or superscripted variables, and bracketed theory-venue citations such as [Author, VENUE'yy]. Score 0 if there is no notation at all and the abstract is entirely prose; score 5 if notation appears occasionally, for example one complexity expression or a couple of symbols; score 10 if notation appears in most sentences and a reader must parse formulas to follow the claims. Count the notation on the page. The judge must NOT judge rigour, correctness, difficulty, or whether formalism is warranted for this topic, and must not treat notation as evidence either for or against the work being good.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 (typography and subject-matter marker). Notation-saturated abstracts sit at the very bottom of the scorecard here: R53 (dense_pct=0.278, card_pct=0.009) is dense with widetilde-O expressions, d, H and epsilon; R48 (0.474 vs 0.021) carries R^d, epsilon-coresets and bracketed SODA/FOCS citations; R04 (0.496 vs 0.120) leads with O(C^2 L^5); R43 (0.389 vs 0.047) and R36 (0.769 vs 0.316) follow the same pattern. A criterion bank written in natural language has nothing to grip when the claim is carried by a symbol, so notation density predicts a low card score for reasons that have nothing to do with the merit of the theorem.
proposals.upstream_parent: writing conventions of the theory-versus-applied subcommunity that produced the work

proposals.name: Enumerated contribution scaffolding and roadmap phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score how much explicit enumerated scaffolding the abstract uses to present its contributions: phrases such as 'our contributions are three-fold' or 'two-fold', sequences of 'First, ... Second, ... Third, ... Fourth, ...', numbered or lettered items such as i) ii) iii) or 1) 2), and explicit roadmap sentences announcing what the paper will do in order. Score 0 when contributions are stated in flowing prose with no enumeration; score 5 when there is one ordinal sequence or a single 'we make two contributions' announcement; score 10 when the body of the abstract is organised as an explicit numbered list. Score only how much of this scaffolding is visible. The judge must NOT decide whether the enumerated contributions are substantial, whether the organisation aids the reader, or whether enumerating is good scientific practice.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 fingerprint of an unseen factor (how practised the group is at writing for this venue's review rubric). Practised submitters pre-chunk the abstract into rubric-shaped slots, which a criterion-bank scorer can tick off one at a time. R12 states 'Our contributions are three-fold' and then walks i)/ii)/iii) (dense_pct=0.291, card_pct=0.594); R28 marches through 'First / Second / Third / Fourth' (0.154 vs 0.641); R51 announces 'Our contribution is two-fold' (0.081 vs 0.564); R29 numbers its findings 1) and 2) (0.605 vs 0.906). Mixed is true and honestly so: a group that has learned the format may also genuinely do better work, so this channel belongs in the sensitivity band rather than being written off.
proposals.upstream_parent: the authors' accumulated practice in this submission format; rubric-aware, reviewer-facing writing habits learned over repeated submission cycles

proposals.name: Roll-call density of named datasets, benchmarks and baseline counts
proposals.instruction: Count how many distinct named datasets, named benchmarks, named architectures and explicit tallies of experimental scope appear in the abstract, and score the density of that roll-call. Named entities include things like MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, GLUE, Omniglot, nuScenes, Argoverse, NTU-60, PKU-MMD, OPUS-100, WMT, Atari 100k, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ResNet-50, and tallies such as '12 baselines, 16 search spaces and 86 datasets' or 'three established datasets'. Score 0 when no dataset or benchmark is named at all; score 5 for one or two names; score 10 when five or more names appear, or when the abstract explicitly totals up the scale of its experimental grid. Count named entities and tallies only. The judge must NOT decide whether the evaluation is adequate, whether the right benchmarks were chosen, or whether more evaluation means better research.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2: the unseen factor is the group's resources, and its textual fingerprint is a long list of names a poorer group could not have run. The roll-call clusters hard on the card-high side: R09 lists MNIST, Omniglot, CIFAR10, DMLab Mazes, Celeb-A and ImageNet32x32 (dense_pct=0.252, card_pct=0.581); R42 advertises 12 baselines, 16 search spaces and 86 datasets (0.385 vs 0.825); R24 names PKU-MMD I, NTU-60 and NTU-120 (0.449 vs 0.833); R08 names GLUE, DistilBERT and RoBERTa (0.372 vs 0.675); R17 names CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet (0.269 vs 0.744). A per-criterion bank almost certainly contains an 'evaluation breadth' item that is satisfied by naming things, so name-counting is being paid for. Mixed is true: resources can buy genuinely better science as well as a longer list.
proposals.upstream_parent: compute budget, engineering staffing and data access available to the producing group

proposals.name: Promotional superlative and novelty vocabulary density
proposals.instruction: Score how heavily the abstract uses promotional and novelty vocabulary, independent of whether the claims behind it are true. Tokens to count include: novel, new (as a boast), state-of-the-art, significantly, substantial, remarkable or remarkably, superior or superiority, extensive, comprehensive, ground-breaking, powerful, promising, effective, 'the first to', 'sheds light on', 'we demonstrate the effectiveness of'. Score 0 for a flat, unmarked descriptive register containing none of these; score 5 when two or three appear; score 10 when such vocabulary appears in most sentences and the abstract reads as continuously self-promoting. The judge must count the vocabulary and NOTHING else: do not check whether the superlatives are earned, do not reward restraint as modesty or penalise boasting as overclaiming, and do not judge the research.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 boilerplate channel, distinct from B03 (which is about structure, not adjectives). Superlative-heavy abstracts concentrate on the card-high side: R14 promises 'remarkable performance gain' and 'state-of-the-art' (dense_pct=0.517, card_pct=0.842); R12 claims 'significant superiority' and 'significantly better performance' (0.291 vs 0.594); R42 'new state-of-the-art results' (0.385 vs 0.825); R24 'outperforms the state-of-the-art' (0.449 vs 0.833); R26 'consistently outperform state-of-the-art' (0.333 vs 0.679). Meanwhile several extreme dense-high items are almost adjective-free: R20 (0.688 vs 0.222) and R22 (0.699 vs 0.145). A judge scoring criteria one by one is reading assertions of merit, and assertion of merit is free to produce.

proposals.name: Visible artifact-release apparatus: URLs, code, weights, video
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of visible artifact-release apparatus in the abstract text: literal URLs to code or model repositories, statements that code, models, data or configuration files are available, promises that they will be released, mentions of pretrained weights, and links to supplementary videos or demos. Score 0 when nothing of the kind appears; score 3 for a bare promise with no link ('we will publicly release the datasets'); score 6 for one explicit URL; score 10 when there is a URL plus several sentences enumerating released assets. Score only the visible presence and amount of release apparatus. The judge must NOT assess whether the artifacts would actually reproduce anything, whether the link looks credible, or whether releasing code makes the research better.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2: two unseen factors (when the work was submitted, and whether the group has engineers who can clean and host a repo) leave one shared fingerprint, a URL in the abstract. Present on card-high items R18 (dense_pct=0.568, card_pct=0.970), R19 (0.218 vs 0.697), R24 (0.449 vs 0.833), R38 (0.214 vs 0.637), R59 (0.094 vs 0.932), R34 (0.573 vs 0.936), plus the weaker unlinked promise in R30 ('We will publicly release both datasets', 0.618 vs 0.295) and the video link in R47 (0.201 vs 0.513). A criterion bank plausibly contains a reproducibility or openness item that a hyperlink satisfies outright. Mixed is true: labs that can release code often do stronger empirical work, so this must appear in both readouts.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission-era release norms at the venue combined with the engineering staffing of the producing lab

proposals.name: Submission-pipeline residue: portal fields and unrendered markup
proposals.instruction: Score how much residue from the submission and ingestion pipeline is visible as literal text. Count: leftover portal field labels pasted into the body, such as 'Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge that I and all co-authors ...' or 'One-sentence Summary: ...'; HTML escape sequences left unrendered, so that > or < appear as literal character sequences where a mathematical symbol was intended; LaTeX source shown raw in running prose, such as emph{...} with visible braces, mathrm, widetilde, or dollar-sign delimiters surrounding a symbol; and stray double spaces, orphaned punctuation or broken parentheses around such fragments. Score 0 for clean, fully rendered text; score 5 for one or two fragments; score 10 when residue appears repeatedly or a whole portal field has been pasted in. Score the amount of residue only. The judge must NOT infer carelessness, sloppiness, rushed work, or anything at all about the quality of the research from it.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, and the parent here is purely mechanical, which is why mixed is false. R29 has an entire portal field pasted onto the end of the abstract, 'Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge ...' followed by 'One-sentence Summary: ...', and sits at card_pct=0.970-adjacent territory (dense_pct=0.605, card_pct=0.906) - extra pasted text gives extra criteria something to score. R08 shows 'k>1' and raw emph{projective clustering} (0.372 vs 0.675); R09 shows '<=41.58 nats/image' (0.252 vs 0.581); R53 shows raw emph{reward-free} and widetilde-O (0.278 vs 0.009). Whether a symbol survived an export step cannot be research quality, but it changes what a text-only scorer sees, and in R29's case it literally adds scorable content.
proposals.upstream_parent: the submission and ingestion pipeline itself: how the venue's portal exported the record and how the author pasted the text in at deadline

proposals.name: Unedited-prose slips: articles, agreement, calqued phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score the extent of unedited-prose features in the abstract: missing, extra or wrong definite and indefinite articles (for example 'The most GCNs suffer the performance loss'); subject-verb or singular-plural disagreement; non-idiomatic verb complements (for example 'we task humans with revise each document'); calqued or word-order-transferred phrasing; stilted coinage introductions such as 'named as X'; and odd capitalisation of a coined term in the title or body. Score 0 for uniformly idiomatic, professionally copy-edited English; score 5 for two or three noticeable slips; score 10 when slips occur several times per paragraph. Count only these mechanical slips. The judge must NOT judge whether the writing is good, whether the authors are competent, or whether the science is sound, and must NOT penalise dense technical jargon, long sentences, or unfamiliar terminology that is grammatically well formed.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2: the unseen factor is who edited the text before submission - a senior co-author, a lab with a house editor, or nobody - and the fingerprint is grammatical residue. R41 has 'The most GCNs suffer the performance loss when the depth of the model increases' (dense_pct=0.618, card_pct=0.141); R30 has 'we task humans with revise each document' (0.618 vs 0.295); R26 uses 'named as ctx-DocNADE' twice and an irregular title capitalisation 'Texttovec' (0.333 vs 0.679); R12's 'either deriving ... , training ... , or directly applying ...' breaks its own parallelism (0.291 vs 0.594). Polish is a proxy for editorial access, not for the validity of the result. Mixed is true because mentorship that buys polish plausibly also improves the research.
proposals.upstream_parent: access to senior co-author polishing or professional copy-editing, and the authors' first language

proposals.name: Narrow-application framing versus general-primitive framing
proposals.instruction: Score how narrowly the abstract scopes the object it is offering. Score 0 when the abstract announces a general-purpose primitive - an estimator, layer, loss, optimiser, bound or attack - that an arbitrary reader in this field could plug into their own setting, with any application mentioned only as illustration. Score 5 when a general mechanism is offered but tied throughout to one family of tasks. Score 10 when the abstract is framed entirely around a single narrow application domain and its domain-specific data and metrics, so that the contribution is legible mainly to specialists in that domain (for example: classifying swim bouts of a particular fish species, predicting vehicle trajectories over road lanes, skeleton-based action recognition, texture synthesis). Score breadth of FRAMING only, from the words on the page. The judge must NOT decide whether broad or narrow work is more valuable, must NOT judge importance or impact, and must NOT reward generality as ambition.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, audience effect. A model that reads raw text end-to-end has absorbed far more surrounding discourse about broadly-adopted primitives than about niche applications, so 'how central is this object to the field' leaks into the text as framing breadth, quite apart from merit. The dense-high extremes all announce general primitives: R46 offers a Transformer attention generalisation (dense_pct=0.996), R58 a defence applicable to any pretrained net (0.991), R15 a general verifier (0.987), R23 a general gradient estimator (0.880), R11 a general attack (0.925). The card-high side is dominated by domain-scoped studies: R16 is about zebrafish swim bouts (0.158 vs 0.756), R14 about vehicle trajectories on lanes (0.517 vs 0.842), R24 about skeleton action representations (0.449 vs 0.833), R37 about ultra-high-resolution segmentation (0.355 card-high side at 0.726). Mixed is true: a general primitive can genuinely be worth more, so this belongs in the sensitivity band.
proposals.upstream_parent: the size and centrality of the audience subcommunity the work addresses, and how much of that audience the reader has already absorbed

proposals.name: Reads as late entrant into an already crowded thread
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the text reads as a late arrival into an already crowded line of work, rather than as one of the first and most obvious readings of its problem. Markers of lateness to count: an opening that enumerates several already-named existing approaches and their shortcomings before the contribution appears; a method or title built explicitly as an increment on a named predecessor (a ++ suffix, 'Extending Y', 'Generalized X', 'Efficient X', 'Simple X', 'A Unified Framework for X', 'A Unified Perspective on X'); explicit positioning against multiple contemporaneous competitors by name; a contribution framed as a fix, unification, stabilisation or extension of things that already exist; hedged differentiation such as 'however, these methods still ...'. Markers of earliness to count in the other direction: the object is introduced with little competitive throat-clearing, the problem is treated as newly posed, and few or no rival named methods are cited. Score 0 for a text that reads as an early, first-pass treatment of its problem, and 10 for one that reads as a late increment inside a saturated thread. You cannot observe the actual submission order or the real crowding of the field - score only the reading the text projects. The judge must NOT decide whether being early or late is better, must NOT judge whether the contribution is incremental in value, and must NOT judge the research.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 (required position channel). The slice separates cleanly along projected position. Late-entrant readings sit dense-low and card-high: R09 is literally titled 'Kanerva++' and defines itself against the Kanerva Machine (dense_pct=0.252, card_pct=0.581); R19 is 'A Unified Algebraic Perspective' that opens by name-checking convex potential layers and Almost-Orthogonal-Layer before proposing its unification (0.218 vs 0.697); R17 positions NeRN as an adaptation of existing neural representations (0.269 vs 0.744); R38 amalgamates a pool of already-published optimisers (0.214 vs 0.637). Early-reading entries sit dense-high: R46 introduces its object in three sentences with no competitive framing (0.996 vs 0.355), R23 poses the categorical-reparameterisation problem as if newly (0.880 vs 0.551), R58 likewise (0.991 vs 0.252). A crowded thread forces an author to spend the abstract on differentiation, which fills exactly the slots a criterion bank scores, while a first-mover has nothing to differentiate against. Mixed is true: arriving early in a thread is correlated with genuinely founding something.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream: how crowded the thread already was when this entry arrived, and where this submission cycle falls in the run of cycles

proposals.name: Unifying theoretical reframing of existing methods
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract offers a genuinely new conceptual lens, equivalence, or unifying formalism that reorganizes how the reader understands an existing problem or family of methods, rather than just combining two known techniques. A 10: the abstract states a specific reframing (e.g., 'we show X is equivalent to Y', 'we interpret Z as an instance of W', a common formalism that subsumes several prior methods). A 0: the abstract simply proposes 'we apply A to B' or 'we combine A and B' with no reinterpretation of the underlying object or problem.
proposals.rationale: R27 generalizes Ollivier-Ricci curvature to hypergraphs via a common theoretical lens grounding disparate prior notions; R50 reinterprets graph convolutions as integral transforms under probability measures, explaining why sampling-based training works; R60 frames its method as a low-pass/high-pass filter trade-off. All three are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this reframing move that a checklist of surface features would miss.

proposals.name: Diagnoses failure mechanism before presenting the fix
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract first isolates a specific, named mechanism by which prior approaches fail (not just 'existing methods are suboptimal') and only then introduces the fix targeted at that mechanism. A 10: the abstract enumerates or names concrete failure mechanisms (e.g., a specific mathematical or behavioral pathology) before the proposed remedy. A 0: the abstract states a method is needed/better with no account of what specifically goes wrong in prior approaches.
proposals.rationale: R54 names three distinct internal failure mechanisms of the Differentiable Neural Computer (lack of key-value separation, de-allocation aliasing, temporal-linkage degradation) before its fixes; R30 diagnoses a specific 'arrogant' behavior in LOLA agents that is 'directly at odds with convergence' before introducing Stable Opponent Shaping. Both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Strength of formal guarantees (proofs, bounds, optimality)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on how strong and explicit the abstract's theoretical guarantees are. A 10: the abstract states a proof of a specific formal property (convergence, stability, optimality, a tight/near-optimal bound) with named conditions under which it holds. A 0: the abstract makes no theoretical claim at all, only empirical performance claims.
proposals.rationale: R41 proves a conditional VAE 'naturally satisfies' formally defined desirable properties for perturbation sets; R43 proves a near-optimal coreset size bound with explicit complexity; R30 proves local convergence to equilibria and avoidance of strict saddles. All are dense_high_card_low, suggesting formal rigor of this kind is under-rewarded by the scorecard relative to the dense model.

proposals.name: Single memorable result vs. scattered number list
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's empirical payoff crystallizes into one crisp, quotable figure or finding versus reading as a list of many disconnected percentage/metric improvements across many settings with no unifying headline. A 10: one dominant, memorable quantitative or qualitative punchline (e.g., a single dramatic speedup or exact figure) that a reader would repeat. A 0: three or more distinct numeric results across different datasets/metrics presented as a flat, undifferentiated list with no headline result singled out.
proposals.rationale: R07 crystallizes its contribution into 'training BERT in 76 minutes' (down from 3 days), and R03 into an exact '4.38%' adversarial-example rate with a certificate for the remainder; both are dense_high_card_low. By contrast R11 lists 1.6% Top-1 gain, 0.16M added parameters, 0.07B FLOPs, and 3-4% box/mask AP gains with no single headline, and R26 lists nats/image figures across six separate benchmarks (MNIST, Omniglot, CIFAR10, DMLab, Celeb-A, ImageNet32x32); both are dense_low_card_high.

proposals.name: Freedom from submission-template boilerplate text
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract text is free of leftover conference-submission-system artifacts (e.g., 'Code of Ethics: I acknowledge...', 'One-sentence Summary:', or similar template scaffolding) that are not part of the actual scientific description. A 10: the text reads as pure scientific prose with no such artifacts. A 0: the abstract visibly contains copy-pasted submission-form boilerplate mixed into the scientific text.
proposals.rationale: R40 embeds an explicit 'Code Of Ethics: I acknowledge that I and all co-authors...' clause and a redundant 'One-sentence Summary:' line directly in the abstract text (dense_low_card_high, card_pct=0.906); by contrast R14 is pure, terse scientific prose with zero extraneous text (dense_high_card_low, dense_pct=0.996).

proposals.name: Generality of claimed scope beyond one case study
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract frames its contribution as applicable to a general class of problems versus scoped to one narrow, specific use case (a single species, a single puzzle game, a single niche dataset) with no broader claim made. A 10: the abstract explicitly claims or demonstrates applicability across a general problem class. A 0: the abstract's contribution and evaluation are confined to one narrow case study with no stated generalization.
proposals.rationale: R04 is scoped entirely to classifying zebrafish swim bouts from one prior SVM study; R16's core demonstration is limited to Sudoku and N-Queens puzzles; R34 is scoped to humanoid motor control. All three are dense_low_card_high, suggesting narrow scope is not penalized by the scorecard the way it may be by the dense model.

proposals.name: Minimalism: removes an assumed-necessary component
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central contribution is showing that a component or assumption widely believed necessary can be removed or simplified while preserving or improving results. A 10: the abstract explicitly frames its finding as eliminating a previously assumed-necessary piece of machinery (e.g., 'needs only X', 'can be fixed without training'). A 0: the contribution only adds new machinery with no simplification framing.
proposals.rationale: R09 shows a GAN for semantic image synthesis 'needs only adversarial supervision', making the long-standard perceptual loss 'superfluous'; R20 argues the final classifier layer 'can be fixed... with little or no loss of accuracy', removing a component assumed to need training. Both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Exactness or certification of central quantitative claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's key quantitative claim is exact, certified, or provably tight rather than an approximate empirical improvement. A 10: the abstract uses language of exactness/certification (e.g., 'exact', 'certificate of', 'near-optimal', a proven tight bound) for its central number. A 0: all quantitative claims are plain empirical deltas (e.g., 'improves accuracy by X%') with no certification or tightness language.
proposals.rationale: R03 reports the 'exact adversarial accuracy' of a classifier together with a formal 'certificate of robustness' for the rest; R43 proves its coreset size is 'near-optimal' and 'nearly-optimal' with explicit stated complexity. Both are dense_high_card_low despite having the most technical, dense abstracts in the slice.

proposals.name: Simple core mechanism with broad empirical validation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 jointly on (a) whether the abstract's central technical idea can be stated in one simple sentence, AND (b) whether that simple idea is then validated across multiple distinct tasks/settings. A 10 requires both: a one-sentence-describable mechanism plus demonstrated breadth of validation. A 0: either the idea requires multiple interacting components to state (not simple) or a simple idea is validated on only one narrow setting (not broad). Partial credit only for satisfying one half.
proposals.rationale: R44's Gumbel-Softmax is a single differentiable relaxation trick validated across structured prediction and unsupervised generative modeling; R07's layerwise-adaptive-rate idea (LAMB) is validated on both BERT and ResNet-50 at large scale. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this simple-idea/broad-validation combination more than the scorecard does.

proposals.name: Named mechanistic contrast with a specific prior method
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 jointly on whether the abstract (a) names a specific prior method by name as its point of comparison, AND (b) gives a mechanistic reason that method falls short (not just a numeric gap). A 10: both a named baseline and a stated mechanistic reason for its shortfall are present. A 0: comparisons are only to generic 'existing methods' or 'baselines' with no named method and no mechanistic reason given.
proposals.rationale: R07 names LARS specifically and states it 'performs poorly for attention models like BERT'; R50 names GCN specifically and explains its 'requirement of simultaneous availability of test data' as the specific limitation being addressed; R30 names LOLA specifically and identifies its 'arrogant' behavior as the specific failure. All three are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Counterintuitive claim that defies a natural prior
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract presents a finding that runs against what a reader would naturally expect going in (a surprising result), versus a finding that confirms the expected direction of improvement. A 10: the abstract explicitly frames its central finding as surprising, counterintuitive, or a 'pitfall' in something believed sound. A 0: the abstract's finding is the expected one (a new method does somewhat better than baselines, as anticipated).
proposals.rationale: R20 argues, against the natural expectation that a large learned classifier head is needed, that it 'can be fixed... with little or no loss of accuracy'; R13 shows the theoretically well-motivated log-likelihood training objective 'can lead to very poor but stable parameter estimates', a pitfall in a method assumed sound. R20 is dense_high_card_low while R13 is dense_low_card_high, indicating this property does not resolve the disagreement in one direction but is nonetheless salient across both extremes of the slice.

proposals.name: Explicit enumerated contribution list ('First,... Second,...')
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10, INVERTED, on the presence of explicit enumeration markers structuring the abstract's contributions (e.g., 'First,... Second,... Third...', '(1)... (2)... (3)...', 'three-fold'). A 10: the abstract reads as continuous prose with no explicit numbered/ordinal contribution list. A 0: the abstract explicitly itemizes three or more contributions or challenges using ordinal or numbered markers.
proposals.rationale: R46 itemizes '(1) No Language Structure in Context... (2) Limited Context and/or Smaller training corpus...'; R48 explicitly frames contributions as 'three-fold' followed by 'First,... Next,... Finally,...' and then '(i)... (ii)... (iii)...'. Both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting the scorecard rewards this checklist structure that the dense model does not.

proposals.name: Resource accounting precision paired with baseline comparison
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 jointly on whether the abstract (a) gives precise resource/complexity accounting (Big-O terms, parameter counts, FLOPs, or wall-clock time), AND (b) anchors that accounting to an explicit named baseline for comparison (not just an absolute number in isolation). A 10: both precise accounting and an explicit before/after or vs.-named-baseline comparison are present. A 0: neither is present, or a number is given with no comparison point.
proposals.rationale: R47 gives explicit complexity terms O(C^2L^5) reduced to O(CL^4) and O(CL^3 log L) relative to the only prior strictly-equivariant layer; R07 gives wall-clock time reduced 'from 3 days to just 76 minutes' relative to standard training. Both are dense_high_card_low.

proposals.name: Claims precisely scoped, not vague superlatives
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether performance claims are stated with precise, falsifiable scope (specific metric, specific magnitude, specific comparison condition) versus unquantified superlative language ('significant', 'remarkable', 'state-of-the-art performance') left unanchored in the abstract itself. A 10: every superlative claim in the abstract is immediately backed by a specific number and comparison condition. A 0: the abstract relies on unquantified superlatives ('significant', 'remarkable', 'superior') without giving the reader a specific figure to evaluate them by.
proposals.rationale: R48 claims 'significant superiority... over baselines' without a figure in the abstract; R58 claims a 'remarkable performance gain' and 'state-of-the-art performance' without quantifying either in the abstract text. Both are dense_low_card_high. By contrast R59 anchors every claim precisely (e.g., '40% embedding-layer reduction with only 0.5% average accuracy drop... compared to a 2.8% drop using the existing SVD approach').

proposals.name: Novelty of the problem formulation itself
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's primary contribution is defining or formalizing a new problem/task (not previously posed in this form) versus proposing a new method for an already well-established, previously-formalized problem. A 10: the abstract explicitly formalizes and names a task or problem setting that did not previously exist as stated. A 0: the abstract targets a long-standing, already-well-defined problem (e.g., standard image classification robustness) with a new method but no new problem formulation.
proposals.rationale: R16 explicitly states it 'formally defines the task of learning one-of-many solutions for combinatorial problems in structured output spaces', a new problem formulation; R23 formalizes 'data-driven algorithm selection and metric learning for clustering problems' as a joint learning problem not previously posed together. Both are dense_low_card_high, indicating the scorecard may credit problem-formulation novelty that the dense model does not weight as heavily as method-level insight.

proposals.name: Abstract length / elaboration verbosity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how long and elaborated the abstract text is (word count, number of sub-clauses/sub-claims covered), where 0 = extremely terse (roughly one to two sentences, under ~60 words) and 10 = extremely long and elaborated (many clauses and sub-claims, over ~250 words). Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the underlying work is good; score length alone.
proposals.rationale: R47 (~55 words, no elaboration) and R05 (~90 words) are both terse and both dense_high_card_low; R35 and R30 are long, heavily elaborated abstracts (multiple numbered sub-problems, many results) and both are dense_low_card_high. A scorecard built from checklist criteria plausibly needs more surface area to find things to score, independent of whether the underlying research is better; but longer abstracts could also genuinely reflect more extensive experiments, so the parent cause is ambiguous (mixed).

proposals.name: Density of numeric performance figures cited
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how many distinct numeric figures (percentages, point-gains, parameter/FLOP counts, dataset/baseline counts, speed multipliers, etc.) appear in the text, where 0 = no numbers at all and 10 = numbers appear in nearly every sentence. Do NOT judge whether the numbers are impressive, large, or correct; score only the density of numeric mentions.
proposals.rationale: R36 (1.6% Top-1, 0.16M params, 0.07B FLOPs, 3-4% AP) and R55 (12 baselines, 16 search spaces, 86 datasets) and R30 (40%, 0.5%, 43%, 0.8%, 3%) are all number-dense and all dense_low_card_high, versus R47, which cites zero numbers and is extremely dense_high_card_low. A checklist scorecard can tick boxes off explicit figures more easily than a holistic reader can; but number density could also genuinely track empirical thoroughness, hence mixed.

proposals.name: Explicit code/model-release repository boilerplate
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how prominently the text advertises a code/model release (an explicit URL, phrases like 'code is available at', 'we release our code/models'), where 0 = no such statement anywhere and 10 = an emphatic, prominently placed release statement. Do NOT judge whether releasing code is good practice or whether the release would be useful; score only the presence/prominence of the boilerplate statement.
proposals.rationale: R17 ('Code is available at https://github.com/ubc-aamodt-group/RLEL_regression') and R24 ('we release our code and models at https://github.com/eloialonso/iris') and R50 ('Code is available at https://github.com/araujoalexandre/...') are all dense_low_card_high, versus R47 and R05, which carry no release statement and are dense_high_card_low. The URL string itself carries no information about the underlying contribution's correctness or novelty, so it is a purely cosmetic template habit rather than a quality-relevant confound.

proposals.name: Ordinal/enumeration scaffolding of contributions or challenges
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the abstract uses explicit ordinal/enumeration markers to organize its claims (e.g., 'First,... Second,...', '(1)...(2)...', 'i)...ii)...iii)', numbered contributions or challenges), where 0 = no ordinal markers at all and 10 = the abstract's structure is built almost entirely around an explicit numbered/ordinal list. Do NOT judge whether the enumerated content itself is good or well-organized in substance; score only the presence of ordinal scaffolding markers.
proposals.rationale: R21 ('First, ... Next, ... Finally, ...' plus 'i) ... ii) ... iii)') and R35 ('(1) No Language Structure ... (2) Limited Context ...') and R39 ('First, we define ... Then, ... Finally, we present ...') all use heavy ordinal scaffolding and are all dense_low_card_high. This is a pure outlining habit independent of the quality of what is being outlined, so purely a nuisance.

proposals.name: Explicit named-predecessor lineage/extension framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how explicitly the text frames the work as a direct successor/extension of one specific, named prior method (e.g., 'In contrast to the Kanerva Machine, we...', 'functional BNNs (fBNNs) address this only partially'), where 0 = no named-predecessor framing at all and 10 = the abstract's central organizing device is an explicit compare-and-extend relationship to one specific named prior system. Do NOT judge whether the extension is actually a genuine improvement over its predecessor; score only how explicitly this named-lineage framing appears in the text.
proposals.rationale: R11 ('Kanerva++', explicitly 'In contrast to the Kanerva Machine, we simplify...') and R08 ('functional BNNs (fBNNs) address this only partially because...') both build their framing around one named predecessor system and are both dense_low_card_high. An author entrenched in a specific line of work leaves this lineage-fingerprint, and such entrenchment could also cause genuinely more mature work, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's established research program / reputation in this specific line of work

proposals.name: Named large-scale engineering/experimental-resource markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the text names concrete large-scale infrastructure or resource figures (specific hardware such as 'TPU Pod', specific huge batch sizes or wall-clock training-time claims, or explicit counts of baselines/search-spaces/datasets used in a single study), where 0 = no such resource/scale figures and 10 = multiple specific large-scale resource figures are named. Do NOT judge whether the scale achieved is impressive or whether more compute makes better research; score only the presence of named resource/scale figures.
proposals.rationale: R14 names specific hardware and scale ('TPUv3 Pod', batch size '32868', 'reduced from 3 days to just 76 minutes') and is dense_high_card_low; R55 advertises an unusually large experimental footprint ('12 baselines, 16 HPO search spaces and 86 datasets/tasks') and is dense_low_card_high. Both leave a textual trace of a well-resourced team, which could be a pure prestige/access signal or could genuinely enable stronger empirical work, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's institutional resources / access to large-scale compute or experimental infrastructure

proposals.name: Head-to-head competitive/marketing rhetorical register
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the text uses head-to-head competitive or marketing-style phrasing against named or generic prior methods (e.g., 'orders of magnitude faster than', 'X times fewer ... than the current state-of-the-art', 'beats the SVM by 6.12%'), where 0 = no comparative/competitive phrasing and 10 = the abstract is saturated with such head-to-head competitive claims. Do NOT judge whether the comparative claims are true, large, or well-supported; score only how much of this competitive rhetorical register is present.
proposals.rationale: R33 ('two to three orders of magnitude quicker than the state-of-the-art') and R29 ('two to four times fewer queries and fail two to five times less often than the current state-of-the-art') and R51 ('our best CNN beats the SVM by 6.12%') all use explicit quantified head-to-head beat-language. This is a subfield writing convention rather than evidence of quality itself, so treated as a pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author/subfield's rhetorical practice in this venue format (marketing-style register common in some subfields, e.g., adversarial robustness/systems, versus a modest descriptive register common in others, e.g., theory)

proposals.name: Self-critical hedging or limitation-naming language
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the text explicitly names a weakness, gap, or limitation of prior approaches or of its own framing using hedging language (e.g., 'address this only partially', 'this depends heavily on...', 'none can offer a universal advantage'), where 0 = no such hedging/limitation language and 10 = the abstract repeatedly and explicitly foregrounds weaknesses or limitations. Do NOT judge whether the acknowledged limitation is actually serious or whether the paper handles it well; score only the presence of the hedging language.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('address this only partially'), R57 ('is random optimal? ... this depends heavily on what functions we are optimizing'), and R39 ('none can offer a universal advantage over other competitive optimizers') all foreground an explicit hedge and are all dense_low_card_high. Hedging could be a pure rhetorical tic that a checklist rewards for 'acknowledging limitations,' or it could genuinely track more careful, self-aware methodology, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's rhetorical/epistemic-honesty norm — practice in this format

proposals.name: Density of formal notation and proof-verb language
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much inline formal notation and proof-oriented verbs appear in the text (e.g., LaTeX-style symbols, Big-O expressions, 'we prove', 'theorem', 'supremum', 'KL divergence equals'), where 0 = no formal notation or proof language at all and 10 = the text is dense with symbolic notation and proof-verbs throughout. Do NOT judge whether the mathematics is correct or the proofs are rigorous; score only the surface density of notation/proof-verb tokens.
proposals.rationale: R27 ('$\widetilde{O}(d^2H^5/\epsilon^2)$', generalized G-optimal design), R58 ('$O(m+poly(k\epsilon^{-1}))$' coreset bounds), R38 ('We give theoretical proof that our method is stable and non-dissipative'), and R03 ('We prove that the KL divergence between stochastic processes equals the supremum...') are all heavily notation/proof-dense and all have extremely low card_pct (0.009-0.034) despite moderate-to-high dense_pct, a striking and consistent pattern. Formal rigor could be genuine theoretical quality that a criterion-bank without a 'proof rigor' item simply cannot capture, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's subfield/training background (theory vs. applied ML) — practice in this format

proposals.name: Crowded-field late-synthesis vs first-mover idea framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how much the abstract frames itself as arriving late into an already-crowded space of many named/enumerated prior alternatives that it must position against, unify, or amalgamate (e.g., 'Existing methods have attempted...', 'Many...have been proposed...however none...', 'amalgamate a pool of teacher optimizers'), versus reading as a direct, minimally-contrastive presentation of one self-contained new idea. Score 0 = reads as a first, direct, minimally-contrastive presentation of an idea; 10 = reads as a late synthesis/differentiation move that explicitly catalogues and positions against many prior alternatives. Do NOT judge whether the positioning against prior work is accurate or whether the synthesis is a genuine advance; score only how much the framing reads as 'early direct idea' vs 'late crowded-field synthesis'.
proposals.rationale: R39 ('Optimizer Amalgamation': explicitly amalgamating 'a pool of teacher optimizers' because 'none can offer a universal advantage') and R50 ('under a common theoretical lens' unifying convex-potential layers, AOL, and orthogonality methods) both read as late syntheses of an already-crowded space and are both dense_low_card_high, versus R47 (a short, direct, uncontested presentation of a new attention mechanism) and R33 ('we determine for the first time...'), both dense_high_card_low. This textual posture reflects where the item sits in the stream of takes on a topic, not the merit of the specific contribution, so purely a nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream — how many similar prior submissions/approaches already existed when this abstract was framed

proposals.name: Problem-to-method fit under realistic failure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete practical or scientific failure and gives a mechanism specifically designed to address it; score 0 when the problem statement and proposed method are only loosely connected or generic.
proposals.rationale: R04 learns perturbations intended to reflect real-world effects, while R31 directly addresses discrete, fluency-constrained NLP attacks. Their dense-high/card-low placement suggests the linkage between failure analysis and method design is underrepresented.

proposals.name: Theory that governs the mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal analysis explains the proposed mechanism, derives its design, and predicts a claimed property; score 0 when theory is absent, ornamental, or disconnected from the algorithm.
proposals.rationale: R01 derives layers from a common SDP condition, R25 connects stability proofs to long-range information preservation, and R48 derives a practical objective from process-level KL theory.

proposals.name: Guarantees under scale and nuisance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a substantive guarantee explicitly survives realistic complications such as outliers, deployment limits, large scale, or unknown rewards; score 0 when guarantees are informal or restricted to an idealized toy setting.
proposals.rationale: R03 combines exact verification with larger networks, R43 addresses deployment and reward uncertainty, and R44 isolates outlier dependence in its coreset bound.

proposals.name: Quantified resource leverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a concrete reduction in time, memory, queries, samples, or deployments and explains what capability that reduction enables; score 0 when efficiency is asserted only vaguely.
proposals.rationale: R16 reports a dramatic training-time reduction, R32 reports orders-of-magnitude graph-training savings, and R39 quantifies query and failure reductions.

proposals.name: Failure-mode diagnosis and targeted repair
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a specific failure, traces its mechanism, and introduces a repair matched to that cause; score 0 when it merely adds a generic component without diagnosing what was broken.
proposals.rationale: R26 names three distinct memory-system failures and supplies corresponding fixes; R45 attributes likelihood-based OOD problems to input complexity; R55 isolates instability caused by the likelihood objective.

proposals.name: Cross-regime evidential robustness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method is tested across genuinely different datasets, tasks, architectures, or operating regimes with a coherent pattern of support; score 0 when evidence comes from one narrow benchmark.
proposals.rationale: R13 spans long and short texts across many datasets, R20 varies architectures and tasks, and R49 studies multilingual directions and data-balance regimes.

proposals.name: Explicit counterfactual or invariance target
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies what should change or remain unchanged under a controlled perturbation and builds the method around that specification; score 0 when it invokes robustness or generalization without defining the relevant transformation.
proposals.rationale: R36 constructs counterfactually revised language data, R47 defines graph augmentation through spectral change, and R45 separates input complexity from distributional novelty.

proposals.name: Mechanistic interpretability that changes design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when analysis reveals what the model uses and that diagnosis leads to a concrete correction, constraint, or design implication; score 0 when interpretability is only descriptive visualization.
proposals.rationale: R19 discovers experimental artifacts and removes them, R36 identifies genre as a spurious signal, and R40 uses classifier analysis to motivate removing a large learned layer.

proposals.name: Plug-in utility with minimal retraining
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the contribution can be applied to pretrained or varied existing systems with little or no task-specific retraining; score 0 when it requires a bespoke end-to-end pipeline for each use.
proposals.rationale: R12 supports on-demand bit widths from one trained model, R46 applies pruning to pretrained networks without fine-tuning, and R40 fixes the classifier while retaining the rest of the network.

proposals.name: Multiplicity and uncertainty representation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly represents multiple valid futures, solutions, or uncertainty states through a distributional or stochastic mechanism; score 0 when it forces a single point answer despite intrinsic ambiguity.
proposals.rationale: R06 models extended imagined futures, R14 models multiple future interactions, R17 handles multiple valid discrete structures, and R54 places uncertainty at the activation level.

proposals.name: Unification yielding new constructions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when prior approaches are placed in a common formal framework that produces genuinely new parameterizations, algorithms, or deductions; score 0 when the claimed unification is merely a relabeling or superficial combination.
proposals.rationale: R01 unifies several Lipschitz constructions and derives new layers, R15 defines several principled optimizer-amalgamation mechanisms, and R35 generalizes curvature from graphs to hypergraphs.

proposals.name: Contextual allocation of capacity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when computation, memory, sampling, or model capacity is allocated conditionally to the instance or context under an explicit constraint; score 0 when allocation is fixed or gating is unmotivated.
proposals.rationale: R05 assigns architectural credit with resource-aware rewards, R27 concentrates sampling on difficult image regions, R49 routes language-specific capacity conditionally, and R57 allocates memory in local blocks.

proposals.name: Ecologically grounded perturbation model
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when perturbations or variation represent plausible changes in the application domain and are tested across multiple such forms; score 0 when they are arbitrary mathematical disturbances with no stated real-world interpretation.
proposals.rationale: R04 models spatial, corruption, and lighting changes, R31 constrains text attacks to fluent perturbations, and R36 uses human-authored counterfactual revisions.

proposals.name: Triangulated evaluation against credible alternatives
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract describes complementary quantitative, qualitative, stress-test, or task-level evaluations against strong alternatives; score 0 when it relies on one metric or unspecified comparisons.
proposals.rationale: R02 combines visual quality with comparisons to classical and neural models, R04 combines quantitative and qualitative perturbation assessment, and R55 uses synthetic and multi-domain tests with predictive and likelihood measures.

proposals.name: Component-level attribution of contribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract separates the roles of major components and provides evidence that each addresses a stated bottleneck; score 0 when a bundled system offers no indication of which parts matter.
proposals.rationale: R05 distinguishes gradient search, credit assignment, and resource constraints; R26 maps three repairs to three diagnosed memory problems; R49 analyzes the effects of routing location and language-specific capacity.

proposals.name: Branded method naming
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the title uses invented acronyms, branded method names, colon subtitles, or self-promotional wording; judge only feature presence, never whether the method is good.
proposals.rationale: Distinctive naming conventions can trigger learned familiarity or novelty heuristics without measuring research quality. Examples include R02's “VariBAD: A Very Good Method” and R31's “Stochastic Activation Pruning.”

proposals.name: Numerical result density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of explicit numerical detail, percentages, benchmark metrics, asymptotic quantities, speedups, or comparative numbers; judge only how much numerical material appears, never whether it is impressive.
proposals.rationale: Some communities habitually foreground quantified results, creating a stylistic signal independent of underlying quality. R10 gives exact batch sizes and training times, while R48 gives percentages, orders of magnitude, and an epsilon value.

proposals.name: Release and resource signaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the abstract advertises code, models, configuration files, datasets, videos, or other reproducibility resources; judge only the presence and prominence of these signals, never their usefulness.
proposals.rationale: Resource-release language can act as an institutional or author-practice cue apart from research quality, although the underlying practice may also support genuine quality. Examples are R16's code, configuration files, and pretrained weights and R57's source code, models, ethics statement, and summary.
