proposals.name: Prior-art anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of named citations, dated references, explicit “recent work” framing, or dense positioning against earlier methods; judge only the amount of bibliographic anchoring, never whether the positioning is correct.
proposals.rationale: Citation density and recency language can reflect field norms or author networks rather than research quality. R08 names and dates Semmelhack et al. (2014), while R34 explicitly surveys several recent approaches before introducing its framework.

proposals.name: Formalism intensity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of displayed notation, asymptotic expressions, named theorems, proof claims, Greek-letter parameters, or highly formal mathematical language; judge only visible formalism, never its validity or importance.
proposals.rationale: Mathematical presentation style can influence text-based reception while only imperfectly tracking research quality, and mathematical training may also affect genuine quality. R50 contains detailed complexity bounds and lower bounds, while R59 uses coreset notation, epsilon guarantees, and poly/k expressions.
proposals.upstream_parent: disciplinary culture and author's mathematical writing practice

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth listing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the abstract enumerates many datasets, tasks, domains, architectures, or application settings; judge only the breadth and count of listed evaluation contexts, never whether the evaluation is sufficient.
proposals.rationale: Long benchmark inventories can signal institutional resources or a field's preferred validation style without directly measuring the contribution, though broad evaluation can also reflect genuine quality. R12 lists MNIST, Omniglot, CIFAR10, DMLab, Celeb-A, and ImageNet, while R25 spans graph classification, molecular prediction, and supervised and semi-supervised settings.

proposals.name: Assertive novelty rhetoric
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of phrases such as “first,” “novel,” “state of the art,” “remarkably,” “only,” “surprisingly,” or other assertive novelty claims; judge only rhetorical frequency, never whether the claims are true or good.
proposals.rationale: Promotional wording can become a nuisance cue because authors and communities differ in how strongly they advertise novelty. R48 says “for the first time” and repeatedly contrasts with the state of the art, while R50 uses “to the best of our knowledge” and “optimal” claims.

proposals.name: Submission-template boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of standardized abstract structure, numbered contribution sequencing, stock transitions such as “in this work,” ethics declarations, one-sentence summaries, or formulaic release statements; judge only templated form, never clarity or quality.
proposals.rationale: Template compliance can create highly predictive wording unrelated to research quality. R27 explicitly says “Our contributions are three-fold,” while R57 includes a Code of Ethics declaration and a labeled One-sentence Summary.

proposals.name: Editing and orthographic artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for visible typos, awkward grammar, inconsistent capitalization, malformed words, punctuation irregularities, or formatting remnants; judge only the amount of such surface variation, never whether the research is good.
proposals.rationale: Copyediting time, text transfer, or formatting pipelines can leave artifacts that a text model detects despite their irrelevance to research quality. R03 contains the awkward phrase “Lacking heretofore have been,” R39 says “The most GCNs,” and R42 begins with the malformed title token “Texttovec.”

proposals.name: Late-synthesis framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract reads like a late-arriving synthesis or extension of an already crowded line, indicated by phrases such as “encompasses existing approaches,” “unifying,” “inspired by,” or repeated contrasts among many predecessors; score only this textual framing, never whether the synthesis is good.
proposals.rationale: An entry written after obvious approaches have occupied the container may linguistically foreground consolidation, extension, or reconciliation; that positional fingerprint is not research quality. R05 says its framework “encompasses various existing approaches,” R34 presents a “unified” perspective on recent methods, and R60 begins from a common compression approach before replacing it.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing

proposals.name: Mechanism–Failure-Mode Fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed mechanism directly targets a specifically diagnosed failure mode; score 0 when it is a generic module attached without a causal connection to the stated problem.
proposals.rationale: R02 links spectral filtering to oversmoothing and neighborhood range; R42 derives memory fixes from diagnosed addressing and de-allocation defects.

proposals.name: Strength of Formal Guarantees
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states substantial, clearly scoped guarantees with explicit assumptions; score 0 when claims are purely empirical or theoretical assertions lack stated conditions.
proposals.rationale: R09 gives deployment and sample-complexity guarantees; R13 and R31 provide convergence, stability, and gradient-preservation claims under broad but specified settings.

proposals.name: Explicit Resource Accounting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when computational, memory, sample, query, or parameter costs are quantified and tied to design choices; score 0 when efficiency is asserted only with vague adjectives.
proposals.rationale: R15 quantifies verifier speed and network scale; R46 gives complexity reductions while explaining how larger expressive models become feasible.

proposals.name: Threat-Model Fidelity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract precisely defines perturbations, attacker access, constraints, and realistic failure modes; score 0 when it invokes robustness without a concrete threat model.
proposals.rationale: R12 specifies training-time structural graph attacks without classifier access; R20 explicitly handles discrete edits, location-content coupling, and fluency constraints.

proposals.name: Failure-Mode and Boundary Disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies important failure mechanisms, limiting regimes, or corrective conditions; score 0 when it presents only benefits with no boundaries or failure analysis.
proposals.rationale: R07 discovers experimental artifacts and corrects them; R26 exposes stable but poor uncertainty estimates and conditions that exacerbate them.

proposals.name: Reproducibility Completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract commits to concrete artifacts such as code, data, configurations, pretrained models, or exact protocols; score 0 when replication-critical details and artifact commitments are absent.
proposals.rationale: R14 provides code, configurations, and pretrained weights; R56 identifies a concrete implementation and publicly available optimizer code.

proposals.name: Theory-to-Algorithm Coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when theoretical analysis directly determines the algorithm or predicts its behavior and the abstract connects both; score 0 when theory and proposed method are unrelated decorations.
proposals.rationale: R04 derives double-descent behavior from influence-function and Hessian analysis; R22 turns a common semidefinite condition into new Lipschitz parameterizations.

proposals.name: Mechanism-Isolating Evaluation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when comparisons or controlled variants isolate which proposed component causes each claimed effect; score 0 when the abstract reports only aggregate comparisons for an inseparable system.
proposals.rationale: R03 contrasts original, counterfactually revised, and combined data to isolate spurious-signal effects; R35 contrasts spectral guidance with generic topology augmentation.

proposals.name: Cross-Regime Reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract explains how the method behaves across materially different tasks, domains, data regimes, or structural conditions; score 0 when breadth is merely a list of settings without reasoning about differences.
proposals.rationale: R18 distinguishes language direction, layer placement, and data imbalance; R40 connects structured exploration in grid worlds with uncertainty-aware behavior in continuous-control domains.

proposals.name: Hidden-Structure Problem Formulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the paper reformulates the task to represent an important latent structure, multiplicity, causality, or interaction that standard formulations omit; score 0 when it merely optimizes the conventional formulation.
proposals.rationale: R45 makes solution multiplicity central to combinatorial learning; R57 formulates causal adjustment through learned conditional mean embeddings rather than density estimation.

proposals.name: Constraint-Aware Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when practical constraints are built into the method's objective, architecture, or operating controls; score 0 when constraints are mentioned only as motivation after the method is fixed.
proposals.rationale: R09 incorporates deployment limits into exploration design; R24 supports on-demand bit-width changes from one trained model, embedding changing resource needs into the method.

proposals.name: Claim–Evaluation Alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every major claim has a directly relevant evaluation or analysis designed for that claim; score 0 when broad benchmark coverage substitutes for testing the central mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R10 claims hybrid reasoning over long-distance structure but gives little mechanism-specific evaluation detail; R50 emphasizes many tasks and baselines while the central ranking hypothesis is less directly isolated.

proposals.name: Closest-Baseline Differentiation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly identifies the nearest competing approach, its precise limitation, and the specific conceptual departure; score 0 when novelty is described mainly as outperforming unspecified state of the art.
proposals.rationale: R25 distinguishes joint algorithm selection from metric learning and names the restricted families; R34 explains how query-driven cross-layer retrieval differs from ordinary layer interaction.

proposals.name: Actionable Interpretability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when interpretation reveals a concrete behavioral cause and leads to correction, diagnosis, or a design insight; score 0 when interpretation is only visualization without actionable consequences.
proposals.rationale: R07 uses relevance maps to find artifacts and remove them; R42 analyzes noisy memory addressing to motivate key-value separation and de-allocation changes.

proposals.name: Claim Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are carefully bounded by assumptions, task scope, and known tradeoffs; score 0 when the abstract uses universal or sweeping language without specifying where the claims apply.
proposals.rationale: R11 explicitly separates one-dimensional, general strongly convex, and quadratic cases; R32 makes broad quality claims across datasets while giving comparatively little discussion of limiting conditions.

proposals.name: Acronym and branding density
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract uses branded method names, acronyms, and stylized title phrasing; judge only presence, not whether the branding is good.
proposals.rationale: Distinctive naming may affect memorability and reception without indicating research quality. Examples include HYSP in R01 and InfoGraph/InfoGraph* in R18.

proposals.name: Quantified comparison density
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract contains numerical gains, percentages, speedups, dataset counts, or explicit baseline comparisons; judge only frequency and prominence, not whether the results are impressive or valid.
proposals.rationale: Dense numerical reporting can attract attention independently of underlying quality. This fingerprint is prominent in R05 and R51.

proposals.name: Artifact availability signaling
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract advertises code, configurations, pretrained models, videos, or other externally accessible artifacts; judge only the presence of such signals, not their usefulness or quality.
proposals.rationale: Authors experienced with conference conventions may include reproducibility-oriented signals that influence reception, while the same practice may also reflect better work. Examples are R06 and R50.

proposals.name: Citation lineage anchoring
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract explicitly names prior authors, named methods, papers, venues, or established research lines; judge only the amount of lineage signaling, not whether the citations are appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Dense anchoring can make an entry appear situated within a recognized community and affect reception without itself establishing quality. Examples include R05 and R15.

proposals.name: Formal mathematical apparatus
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract uses equations, asymptotic complexity, theorem or proof language, formal assumptions, or named mathematical objects; judge only visible formalism, not correctness or sophistication.
proposals.rationale: Mathematical presentation style can trigger favorable or unfavorable reactions independently of substantive quality, although mathematical fluency may also correlate with quality. Examples are R03 and R60.

proposals.name: Template residue and copy-edit variation
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract contains boilerplate sections, unusual capitalization, typographical inconsistencies, abrupt wording, or visibly inherited template language; judge only textual consistency, not writing quality.
proposals.rationale: Different editing workflows can leave visible residue that affects reception, while editing resources may also influence the underlying work. Examples include the capitalization irregularity in R01 and the template-like ethics and summary text in R50.

proposals.name: Fashionable topic alignment
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract foregrounds currently salient topics, model families, benchmarks, or trend-associated terminology; judge only topical alignment, not whether the topic is important or the method is good.
proposals.rationale: Alignment with community fashion may increase attention independently of quality, while topic choice can also reflect genuine expertise. Examples include Transformer and Atari framing in R38 and graph contrastive learning terminology in R35.

proposals.name: Recency and novelty framing
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract uses temporal or novelty cues such as recent, emerging, current, first, new, state of the art, or previously unexplored; judge only the extent of such wording, not whether the novelty claim is true.
proposals.rationale: Recency-sensitive framing can benefit from attention cycles and timing effects without changing research quality. Examples include R21's recent-success framing and R35's emerging-technique framing.

proposals.name: Obvious-take versus late-riff framing
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract reads as either a direct, obvious response to a standard problem or a later riff that explicitly extends, fixes, unifies, or challenges an already familiar line; judge only the rhetorical position expressed in the text, not actual submission order or originality.
proposals.rationale: An entry's unseen position in a crowded stream could leave a textual trace through direct problem framing versus explicit corrective or integrative framing, affecting reception without quality. Examples include the direct task definition in R04 and the explicit extension framing in R33.

proposals.name: Jargon and compound-term load
proposals.instruction: Assign 0–10 for how much the abstract relies on unexplained technical noun compounds, stacked modifiers, specialized abbreviations, and dense field-specific terminology; judge only linguistic density, not clarity or technical merit.
proposals.rationale: Field-specific lexical density can cue insider familiarity or outsider difficulty independently of quality. Examples include R14's anti-symmetric DGN terminology and R26's hypergraph curvature terminology.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Diagnosis of Prior Failures
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text pinpoints the exact mathematical, architectural, or dynamical root cause of failure in established methods. Score 0 if it introduces a new method without explaining why prior methods fail mechanistically.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values surgical critiques of existing architectures. For example, R03 identifies the exact memory aliasing and flat address distribution flaws in DNCs, and R08 pinpoints the arrogant behavior in LOLLA algorithms, whereas R01 and R07 lack this mechanistic diagnosis.

proposals.name: Provable Theoretical Guarantees
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly proves a convergence guarantee, sample complexity bound, or information-theoretic limit within the text. Score 0 if it relies entirely on empirical observations and metrics without formal theoretical claims.
proposals.rationale: The dense model heavily favors rigorous theoretical proofs over empirical heuristics. R06 proves the KL divergence equivalence in functional BNNs, R11 proves the near-optimal coreset size, and R55 provides information-theoretic lower bounds. The scorecard misses this depth in favor of empirical methods like R24 and R44.

proposals.name: Principled Architectural Simplification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if state-of-the-art results are achieved by mathematically redesigning the model to explicitly remove ad-hoc components or auxiliary loss terms. Score 0 if performance is improved solely by adding heuristic modules, extra layers, or complex auxiliary losses.
proposals.rationale: The dense model recognizes mathematical elegance in removing unnecessary components. R14 mathematically redesigns the discriminator to make the VGG-based perceptual loss superfluous, and R32 fixes the classifier layer to eliminate vast parameters. Conversely, the scorecard likely over-credits the heuristic complexity seen in R42 and R52.

proposals.name: Formal Mathematical Bridging Across Domains
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a concept from a distinct field is formally mapped to the target problem via rigorous mathematical instantiation. Score 0 if inspiration is drawn from another field superficially using loose terminology without formal mathematical mappings.
proposals.rationale: The dense model credits formal mathematical mapping over superficial analogy. R09 maps adversarial defense to a game-theoretic minimax mixed strategy, and R28 maps hypergraph structure to Ollivier-Ricci curvature via optimal transport. This contrasts with the vague biological or cognitive analogies in R23 and R26.

proposals.name: Derivation of Symmetry Constraints
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if necessary equivariance, invariance, or geometric constraints are explicitly derived and strictly enforced into the model's mathematical formulation. Score 0 if standard architectures are used and symmetries are left to be implicitly learned from data.
proposals.rationale: The dense model identifies high value in mathematically constraining the hypothesis space. R22 explicitly derives strictly equivariant spherical CNN layers with reduced complexity, and R33 finds a principled way to guide topology augmentations by exploring spectral invariance, moving beyond the standard black-box approaches seen in R43.

proposals.name: Fundamental Objective Space Reformulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the problem is fundamentally reformulated by changing the underlying mathematical space of optimization (e.g., from weights to functions, or spatial to spectral). Score 0 if standard objectives are optimized natively via minor algorithmic tweaks.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards shifting the mathematical foundations of the problem. R06 moves Bayesian inference from the weight space to the function space via stochastic processes, and R10 reformulates Neural Architecture Search as an optimization problem on joint distributions, surpassing the standard parameter-tuning seen in R12.

proposals.name: Exact Analytical Relaxation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a discrete or non-differentiable operation is replaced by a continuous surrogate alongside a formal proof of equivalence or bounded approximation error. Score 0 if heuristic approximations or surrogates are used without formal mathematical equivalence.
proposals.rationale: Making the discrete differentiable via provable relaxation is highly valued by the dense model. R13 introduces the Gumbel-Softmax to smoothly anneal into a categorical distribution, and R16 uses convex relaxation to co-optimize discrete text perturbations, contrasting with the ad-hoc surrogates in R50.

proposals.name: Explicit Complexity Bound Reduction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text explicitly reduces theoretical computational complexity (e.g., Big-O notation) and proves how the new architecture achieves this bound. Score 0 if only empirical wall-clock speedups or memory reductions are reported.
proposals.rationale: The dense model credits formal algorithmic improvements over empirical benchmarking. R22 explicitly reduces the complexity of spherical CNNs from O(C^2L^5) to O(CL^3 log L), and R34 achieves computational speedups via tight mathematical formulations for non-linearities in MIP solvers.

proposals.name: Decomposition of Core Mathematical Trade-offs
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the work isolates and theoretically analyzes the interaction between two fundamental opposing forces (e.g., exploration vs exploitation, bias vs variance, smoothness vs over-squashing). Score 0 if performance is treated as a monolithic entity without analyzing internal trade-offs.
proposals.rationale: Analyzing the tension between opposing mathematical forces is a hallmark of high-quality research detected by the dense model. R05 analyzes the trade-off in layer-wise adaptation for large-batch training, and R19 investigates how the loss function affects the double descent phenomena via the Hessian spectrum.

proposals.name: Unified Algebraic or Geometric Generalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a single mathematical framework strictly subsumes and generalizes multiple existing disparate methods into one cohesive formulation. Score 0 if the proposed method is an isolated formulation that ignores its mathematical relationship to prior art.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values unifying disparate literature under a rigorous mathematical lens. R28 creates a unified framework generalizing curvature to hypergraphs. Conversely, the scorecard over-credits R58, which attempts an algebraic unification of Lipschitz networks but lacks the deeper algorithmic novelty perceived by the dense model.

proposals.name: Theoretical Validation of Representations
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if there is a formal mathematical proof that a learned representation or embedding strictly preserves a crucial property of the underlying data (e.g., mutual information, distance metrics). Score 0 if representations are only evaluated empirically on downstream tasks.
proposals.rationale: The dense model prioritizes formal validation of latent spaces. R21 derives the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality to ensure the network approximates the Partial Wasserstein discrepancy, and R31 maximizes the mutual information between graph-level and substructural representations with theoretical backing.

proposals.name: First-Principles Continuous Formulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the architecture is derived directly from first principles, such as continuous ordinary/partial differential equations or dynamical systems. Score 0 if the architecture is constructed by stacking discrete heuristic blocks based solely on empirical performance.
proposals.rationale: The dense model assigns high quality to architectures rooted in continuous mathematics. R39 interprets graph convolutions as integral transforms under probability measures, and R49 designs stable graph networks through the lens of ordinary differential equations, avoiding the fragility of purely discrete architectural hacks.

proposals.name: Rigorous Bilevel Optimization Resolution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a complex learning problem is formulated and rigorously solved as a bilevel optimization program (e.g., meta-learning via meta-gradients). Score 0 if single-level objectives are optimized or alternating heuristic updates are used without formal bilevel integration.
proposals.rationale: Formulating hierarchical learning problems via exact bilevel optimization is credited by the dense model. R20 uses meta-gradients to solve the bilevel problem underlying training-time attacks, and R40 meta-learns approximate inference to rigorously solve Bayes-adaptive deep RL.

proposals.name: Axiomatic Objective Derivation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the learning objective or loss function is rigorously derived from a stated set of mathematical axioms or desired invariance properties. Score 0 if standard off-the-shelf loss functions are used or modified via unprincipled heuristics and weighting terms.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards losses derived from axioms rather than heuristics. R48 formulates desirable properties to measure a perturbation set and mathematically proves a CVAE satisfies them. Conversely, the dense model sees little value in R27 and R18, which rely on heuristic surrogate weighting or post-hoc regularizers.

proposals.name: Information-Theoretic Grounding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the model's formulation is explicitly grounded in information-theoretic principles (e.g., maximum entropy, mutual information maximization, KL divergence) with formal derivations. Score 0 if the formulation relies on standard statistical pattern matching without information-theoretic justifications.
proposals.rationale: Grounding the model in information theory is a strong indicator of quality for the dense model. R13 leverages probability theory to formally define its gradient estimator, and R31 explicitly bases its graph-level representation learning on mutual information maximization, unlike the ad-hoc modeling in R45 and R51.

proposals.name: Raw math typesetting artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text contains raw LaTeX math commands or symbols (e.g., $x$, \epsilon, \mathbb{R}) inline. Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Theoretical papers often leave raw LaTeX in the abstract (R41, R53), which might unfairly confuse dense models evaluating text fluency, though theoretical depth can correlate with genuine quality.

proposals.name: Explicit code release boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text contains boilerplate sentences explicitly providing URLs to GitHub repositories or promising open-source code. Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Well-resourced labs frequently include explicit GitHub links at the end of abstracts (R04, R18), signaling institutional support that predicts reception but is not the core research idea itself.

proposals.name: Hyperbolic scaling language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the abstract uses dramatic or hyperbolic language regarding computation time, efficiency, or scale (e.g., 'massive', 'orders of magnitude'). Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts emphasizing extreme computational speedups or scale often reflect industry PR practices (R08, R11), acting as a fingerprint for corporate backing which influences reception but is a nuisance feature.

proposals.name: Archaic or idiosyncratic phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text uses archaic, awkward, or highly idiosyncratic phrasing (e.g., 'lacking heretofore'). Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Unusual phrasing or convoluted syntax (R06, R38) leaves a textual fingerprint of non-native drafting or lack of professional copyediting, acting purely as a nuisance bias against otherwise valid work.

proposals.name: Conference template boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text includes explicit boilerplate from conference submission templates (e.g., 'One-sentence summary', 'Code of Ethics'). Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Inclusion of specific OpenReview template fields like 'One-sentence Summary' (R54) indicates author familiarity with the venue's exact process mechanics, a nuisance process factor unrelated to quality.

proposals.name: Forced acronym or portmanteau
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text introduces a forced, capitalized acronym or catchy portmanteau (e.g., FastGCN, NeRN) for the proposed method. Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Authors often coin forced acronyms or portmanteaus to improve memorability (R01, R26); this marketing practice may predict how a paper is received but the name itself is not research quality.

proposals.name: Idiomatic or pun-based titles
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the title relies on an idiom, pun, or pop-culture reference (e.g., 'Prior Convictions') rather than a literal description. Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Titles that use puns or idioms (R28, R42) are rhetorical devices reflecting an author's stylistic choice to stand out, acting as a stylistic nuisance rather than a measure of underlying quality.

proposals.name: X meets Y cross-pollination framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text is framed explicitly as combining two distinct, established fields or methods in a formulaic 'X meets Y' structure. Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Framing a paper as a collision of two existing buzzwords (R12, R38) often signals a late-arriving entry trying to find an open niche in the literature, representing crowdedness rather than core quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: Position in the entry stream (late-arriving riff)

proposals.name: Obvious take unifying framework framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text frames a straightforward baseline or obvious extension as a grand, unifying framework. Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Presenting standard combinations as novel unifying frameworks (R34, R48) is characteristic of an early, obvious take on a prompt, representing a positional artifact in the idea stream rather than quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: Position in the entry stream (early obvious take)

proposals.name: Early citation name-dropping
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on the extent to which the text explicitly names a specific prior author or model (e.g., 'Kipf and Welling') in the very first sentence. Do not judge whether this makes the paper better or worse.
proposals.rationale: Opening directly with a specific author name-drop (R01, R59) is a stylistic habit dictated by subfield norms or personal writing practice, functioning purely as a surface-level community marker.

proposals.name: Formal guarantee with tightness evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract states a formal theoretical guarantee (convergence, approximation bound, complexity result, etc.) AND provides evidence the guarantee is tight or near-optimal (matching lower bound, optimality argument, comparison to information-theoretic limits). Score 0 if no formal guarantee of any kind is stated.
proposals.rationale: R17 explicitly shows its coreset size dependence on outliers is 'nearly-optimal' with a lower-bound argument, and R31 claims 'optimal deployment complexity and optimal d dependence' simultaneously for the first time. The dense model likely rewards proofs accompanied by tightness analysis—something a checklist may not distinguish from proofs that merely exist.

proposals.name: Novel mathematical abstraction introduced
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper introduces a genuinely new mathematical object, operator, or formalism not previously seen in the literature (e.g., a new attention mechanism grounded in algebraic topology, a new divergence on stochastic processes). Score 0 if the paper uses only standard, off-the-shelf mathematical tools in conventional ways.
proposals.rationale: R08 introduces 2-simplicial attention generalising dot-product attention via tensor products, and R44 defines a functional ELBO directly on stochastic processes with a novel KL-divergence representation theorem. The dense model perceives genuine mathematical novelty that a scorecard counting surface-level criteria may miss.

proposals.name: Core claim challenges conventional wisdom
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the central result of the paper would surprise a knowledgeable practitioner or overturn a widely held assumption (e.g., 'you do not need X that everyone uses'). Score 0 if the result confirms what most researchers would already expect.
proposals.rationale: R11 shows perceptual loss is 'superfluous' for semantic image synthesis—contrary to established practice—and R36 argues the entire final classifier layer can be fixed random with no accuracy loss. The dense model likely up-weights surprising findings regardless of benchmark breadth.

proposals.name: Method derived from first principles
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed method follows logically and step-by-step from a fundamental mathematical or physical principle stated in the abstract (e.g., loss Taylor expansion → regulariser; piecewise-linear structure → MIP). Score 0 if the method is introduced heuristically or by analogy, with justification added post hoc.
proposals.rationale: R23 derives the ℓ1-gradient regulariser directly from the first-order term of the loss expansion under quantization modelling, and R40 formulates network verification as an MIP by exploiting the piecewise-linear structure of ReLU networks. The dense model rewards derivation chains a scorecard may not distinguish from motivated guesses.

proposals.name: Precise mechanistic diagnosis before solution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract pinpoints the exact mechanism causing prior methods to fail (named, characterised, and specific) before proposing a fix. Score 0 if the problem statement is generic ('X is slow/inaccurate') with no mechanistic explanation.
proposals.rationale: R02 identifies LOLA's specific 'arrogant behaviour' that is 'directly at odds with convergence,' and R45 names three precise DNC pathologies (lack of key-value separation, memory aliasing, temporal-linkage degradation) before proposing targeted fixes. The dense model rewards diagnostic precision that a scorecard might conflate with generic problem-motivation.

proposals.name: Simpler method enabled by deeper understanding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper achieves comparable or better results with a structurally simpler method than prior work, AND this simplification is enabled by a new theoretical insight. Score 0 if improvement comes solely from adding more components, parameters, or engineering complexity.
proposals.rationale: R10 shows a linear learner on spectral graph convolution is competitive, enabled by spectral analysis revealing low-pass/high-pass trade-offs, and R36 replaces a trained classifier with a fixed Hadamard matrix, enabled by the insight that the classifier's value is marginal. The dense model likely credits insight-driven simplification that a scorecard may not distinguish from mere architectural change.

proposals.name: Foundational tool reusability potential
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core technique is general enough to become a standard building block reused across many future papers and subfields (e.g., a new gradient estimator, a new optimiser, a new training trick). Score 0 if the technique is tightly coupled to one task, dataset family, or architectural variant.
proposals.rationale: R49 (Gumbel-Softmax) provides a differentiable sampling mechanism reusable wherever categorical latents appear, and R50 (LAMB) provides a layerwise adaptive optimiser applicable to any large-batch training regime. The dense model perceives trans-scenario utility that a scorecard focused on within-paper results may miss.

proposals.name: Non-trivial conceptual bridge across subfields
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper connects two or more ML subfields or external mathematical disciplines in a way that is both novel and productive (e.g., causality → NLP, ODE stability → graph networks). Score 0 if the paper stays entirely within one established subfield using its standard tools.
proposals.rationale: R26 reframes spurious correlations in NLP through the language of causal inference (back-door/front-door adjustment), and R55 imports anti-symmetric ODE design into deep graph networks to guarantee non-dissipativity. The dense model rewards cross-pollination that a scorecard may not credit if its criteria are organised by subfield.

proposals.name: Prior approaches shown as special cases
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper's framework demonstrably subsumes multiple prior methods as special cases or instances of a single more general formulation. Score 0 if the paper proposes yet another method alongside existing ones without any unifying relationship.
proposals.rationale: R53 generalises Ollivier-Ricci curvature from graphs to hypergraphs in a framework that recovers prior graph curvature as a special case, and R47 presents a generalised spherical CNN framework that 'encompasses various existing approaches.' The dense model credits unification that a scorecard counting 'novelty' generically may miss.

proposals.name: Previously unrecognized problem formalized
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper identifies, names, and formally defines a problem that the community had not previously studied or had studied only informally. Score 0 if the paper works on a long-established, well-formalized problem.
proposals.rationale: R25 identifies that training-time attacks on graph neural networks via structure perturbation are unstudied and formalises the bilevel optimisation, and R30 identifies and formalises the gap between real-world perturbations and the narrowly defined sets used in adversarial-robustness research. The dense model rewards problem-creation that a scorecard may not distinguish from problem-solving.

proposals.name: Theory directly produces the algorithm
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the theoretical analysis is not merely a companion to the method but is the direct source of the algorithmic design (the math tells you exactly what to do). Score 0 if the theory and the algorithm are presented separately, with theory serving as post-hoc justification.
proposals.rationale: R40's MIP formulation of piecewise-linear network verification directly yields the verifier algorithm, including the presolve and tight ReLU formulations, and R31's deployment-complexity analysis directly dictates the exploration-preserving policy discretisation and G-optimal design. The dense model rewards tight theory-algorithm coupling that a scorecard may rate as just 'theoretically grounded.'

proposals.name: Single crystalline insight driving the paper
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the entire paper is driven by one clearly identifiable intellectual insight from which the method, analysis, and experiments all follow naturally. Score 0 if the paper accumulates multiple independent components or techniques without a unifying idea.
proposals.rationale: R49's single insight—replacing non-differentiable categorical samples with a differentiable Gumbel-Softmax relaxation—drives the entire contribution, and R08's single idea—higher-dimensional (2-simplicial) attention—generates both the architecture and its logical-reasoning application. Contrast with dense_low items like R03 or R07 that list many components. The dense model rewards intellectual unity.

proposals.name: Benchmark SOTA claims without explanatory mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 (HIGH = scorecard over-credits) if the abstract's primary selling points are state-of-the-art numbers or leaderboard rankings with little or no explanation of WHY the method works. Score 0 if every performance claim is accompanied by a mechanistic explanation.
proposals.rationale: R04 leads with 'mean human normalized score of 1.046' and 'outperforms humans on 10 out of 26 games' but offers no deep explanation of why Transformers make good world models, and R20 reports '1.6% Top-1 accuracy' and '3-4% box AP' improvements without explaining mechanistically why cross-layer attention helps. The scorecard likely credits SOTA claims; the dense model does not when mechanism is absent.

proposals.name: Method combination without unifying theoretical principle
proposals.instruction: Score 10 (HIGH = scorecard over-credits) if the paper's method is primarily a combination, integration, or amalgamation of existing techniques without introducing a new theoretical principle that explains why this combination is principled rather than merely effective. Score 0 if the combination is derived from or justified by a novel theoretical principle.
proposals.rationale: R12 amalgamates analytical optimizers via a learnable target without a theoretical principle explaining when and why amalgamation helps, and R51 combines genetic algorithms, imitation learning, and policy gradient methods for RL without a unifying theoretical framework. The scorecard likely rewards the engineering of combination; the dense model discounts it absent principled justification.

proposals.name: Contribution centred on domain application over transferable methodology
proposals.instruction: Score 10 (HIGH = scorecard over-credits) if the paper's main value proposition is solving a specific application-domain problem (e.g., a particular species, vehicle type, or clinical task) with methods that are standard or slightly adapted, rather than introducing methodology that transfers broadly. Score 0 if the method is explicitly designed to be domain-agnostic and broadly applicable.
proposals.rationale: R46 applies CNNs and Deep Taylor Decomposition to zebrafish swim-bout classification—a contribution centred on the biological domain rather than on transferable ML methodology, and R59 focuses on vehicle trajectory prediction with lane-level reasoning specific to driving domains. The scorecard likely credits clear domain results; the dense model appears to discount narrow applicability.

proposals.name: Acronym Coining Density
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the text introduces and repeatedly uses custom acronyms for proposed methods or concepts (e.g., 'A-DGN', 'NeRN'). 0 means no custom acronyms are used; 10 means the text is heavily reliant on multiple, newly defined acronyms. Do not judge if the acronym is good or clever, only quantify its presence.
proposals.rationale: The practice of branding a method with an acronym often serves as a strong signal of a distinct contribution to surface pattern models, independent of the underlying quality. R01 (A-DGN) and R03 (NeRN) both introduce heavy acronyms, potentially biasing models that key onto named entities rather than assessing true research depth.

proposals.name: Code Repository URL Inclusion
proposals.instruction: Score the presence and prominence of a URL pointing to an external code repository (like GitHub) within the text. 0 means no URL is present; 10 means a prominent, explicitly highlighted URL is included as a core feature. Do not evaluate the quality or validity of the code, only its textual presence.
proposals.rationale: The mere mention of a code release is a formatting choice that can act as a proxy for completeness, which text models might over-reward without evaluating the actual paper's rigor. R28 and R60 both prominently feature GitHub links, a surface artifact that can be decoupled from the actual research quality.

proposals.name: LaTeX Syntax Leakage
proposals.instruction: Rate how much raw, uncompiled LaTeX or markup syntax (e.g., \emph{}, $...$, <, >) is visible in the text. 0 means perfectly clean, compiled text; 10 means the text is heavily cluttered with raw code artifacts. Do not penalize the text, merely quantify the volume of formatting leakage.
proposals.rationale: Differences in how the text was extracted, submitted, or proofread leave explicit markup artifacts that text models easily latch onto as proxies for careful editing or specific sub-fields. R02 and R26 contain explicit LaTeX commands like \emph and math environments, an artifact of upstream document processing rather than research quality.

proposals.name: SOTA and Superlative Hype Phrasing
proposals.instruction: To what extent does the text use superlative or definitive competitive phrasing (e.g., 'state-of-the-art', 'novel', 'superior performance', 'remarkable performance gain')? 0 means purely objective, restrained language; 10 means heavily loaded with hype and superlatives. Do not judge if the claims are true, only count the frequency and intensity of these phrases.
proposals.rationale: Aggressive marketing practices or lab cultures that push for strong rhetorical claims can cause a model to perceive higher value simply through assertive phrasing. R04 and R21 make sweeping claims of 'new state-of-the-art results' and 'remarkable performance gain' that might impress a model regardless of the actual marginal improvement.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's marketing practice or lab culture

proposals.name: Interdisciplinary Analogy Framing
proposals.instruction: Score how heavily the text frames its machine learning contribution using analogies, structural comparisons, or terminology imported from unrelated scientific fields (e.g., biology, neuroscience, physics). 0 means standard ML terminology only; 10 means heavily reliant on external field jargon. Do not judge the validity of the analogy, only its prominence.
proposals.rationale: Authors with interdisciplinary backgrounds often map ML concepts to physical or biological processes, creating a textual fingerprint of novelty that may not reflect actual algorithmic quality. R37 draws heavily from geometry and topology, while R40 explicitly borrows 'heap allocation' from computer science and 'episodic memory' from neuroscience.

proposals.name: Late-Arriving Trend Adoption Phrasing
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract reads as a late-arriving riff on an established trend, heavily anchoring its motivation on explicitly citing 'recent' surges, specific named prior architectures, or the 'recent success of X'. 0 means it does not anchor on recent trends; 10 means it is explicitly positioned as a direct extension of a current fad. Do not judge novelty, only the textual fingerprint of trend-following.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts written later in a trend cycle often explicitly position themselves against the obvious baseline of the moment, leaving a textual tell of their submission timing. R39 references the 'recent surge in interest' for LARS, and R60 bases its whole premise on the 'success of Transformers', marking them as late-arriving riffs on an existing wave rather than foundational work.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the research entry stream

proposals.name: Conference Boilerplate Inclusion
proposals.instruction: How much of the text consists of standard conference submission boilerplate (e.g., Code of Ethics acknowledgements, 'One-sentence Summary', conflict of interest statements) accidentally included in the abstract? 0 means no boilerplate; 10 means the abstract is heavily cluttered with administrative noise. Do not judge the author's compliance, only the volume of this text.
proposals.rationale: Artifacts of the submission portal or copy-paste errors by the authors leave administrative fingerprints that have zero correlation with research quality but heavily distract text models. R49 contains explicit 'Code Of Ethics' and 'One-sentence Summary' fields, clearly an artifact of the upstream submission process bleeding into the text.

proposals.name: Buzzword Stacking Density
proposals.instruction: Score the density of popular, high-frequency machine learning buzzwords (e.g., Transformer, Reinforcement Learning, Attention, Generative, Deep) packed closely together in the first few sentences. 0 means sparse, specific terminology; 10 means a dense clustering of buzzwords. Do not judge relevance, only the extent of buzzword clustering.
proposals.rationale: Authors writing for maximum visibility or targeting broad audiences often stack searchable keywords, creating a textual fingerprint of audience optimization. R03 and R60 pack their openings with dense combinations of terms like 'Neural Representations', 'convolutional neural network', 'Transformers', and 'world model', optimizing for keyword recognition over focused scientific communication.

proposals.name: Heavy Compute Infrastructure Boasting
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the text explicitly emphasizes massive computational scale or specialized industrial hardware (e.g., 'TPU Pod', 'massive datasets', 'large-scale experimental protocol'). 0 means no mention of scale; 10 means the abstract foregrounds industrial compute as a main selling point. Do not judge if the scale is necessary, only how much it is textually foregrounded.
proposals.rationale: Well-funded labs can leverage massive compute, and they often leave a textual fingerprint by boasting about infrastructure scale, which models may misread as inherent algorithmic quality. R04 brags about a protocol with '86 datasets/tasks', while R39 explicitly foregrounds the 'memory limit of a TPUv3 Pod' as a core narrative element.

proposals.name: Abstract Math Notation Density
proposals.instruction: How much formal mathematical notation (equations, variables, sets) is explicitly written into the abstract text itself? 0 means purely prose; 10 means the abstract is heavily equation-laden. Do not judge the mathematical correctness or complexity, only the visual density of math symbols.
